analysis.one_liner: Creates federal grants so states can make community college tuition-free and give students emergency aid.
analysis.headline: The bill never got past a committee referral; it was introduced in late September 2022 and the 117th Congress ended without any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set up four federal grant programs. The largest would give every state that applied full federal funding for five years to eliminate tuition and fees at its community colleges for eligible adult students without a credential. A second program would fund colleges to hire counselors, navigators, and staff and provide supports like childcare, transportation, and housing help; a third would give emergency cash grants of up to $1,500 per year ($2,500 for student parents) to students facing eviction, food insecurity, lost childcare, or a medical crisis; and a fourth would fund technical help for states writing the applications. States would also have to guarantee that community college credits transfer to public four-year universities.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults at least 18 who live in a participating state and do not already have a college credential, including people without a high school diploma, low-income workers, and first-generation students. They would pay no tuition or fees at community colleges, get help with childcare, transportation, and housing through campus navigators, and could receive emergency grants if a job loss, utility shutoff, or medical problem threatened their enrollment. Students would also get guaranteed credit transfer to public four-year universities, so a two-year degree counts as the first half of a bachelor's. States get funding weighted toward those with higher unemployment and poverty.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates tuition and fees at community colleges for eligible students, with the federal government covering 100% of the cost for the first five years of each state grant.

Provides emergency aid subgrants of up to $1,500 per academic year ($2,500 for students with dependents) to public college students facing job loss, food insecurity, housing or childcare crises, or medical needs, and the aid would not count as taxable income.

Funds colleges in high-poverty areas and at historically Black, Hispanic-serving, Tribal, rural, and other minority-serving institutions to hire career counselors and navigators and centralize support services, with states required to report results broken down by race, ethnicity, and income.

Requires states to guarantee that an associate's degree fully transfers as the first two years of a related bachelor's program at any public university in the state, with common course numbering so credits are not lost.

Directs states to prioritize people with employment barriers or incomes below 200% of the poverty level, and to let enrollment in a credential program count toward work requirements in welfare, SNAP, and childcare programs.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the grants, with open-ended appropriations authorized for five fiscal years. States would be expected to plan how to sustain tuition-free college after the federal money runs out. If tuition-free public college drew students away from them, for-profit colleges and other institutions charging tuition could lose enrollment and revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes unlimited federal spending ('such sums as are necessary') for five fiscal years with no cost estimate, and states are only asked, not required, to sustain tuition-free college after the five-year federal grant period ends, raising the question of what happens when the money runs out.

The free tuition applies only to students without any existing postsecondary credential, and the bill's definition of eligible institutions for the main tuition program is built around community colleges, so adults who already hold a credential and students at private or for-profit colleges get no direct benefit even if they face the same cost barriers.

Implementation depends on states designing interagency committees, data-sharing agreements, and transfer agreements; states that apply slowly or build weak plans could delay or dilute the benefit for their residents.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete for the people it covers: a free path to a two-year credential, guaranteed transfer to a four-year degree, and cash help in a crisis. The main honest concerns are fiscal and structural — the bill sets no spending ceiling and does not guarantee states keep the program running after federal funds end, and it helps only people who do not yet have a credential. On the merits it is a well-targeted expansion for low-income and working adults, but it never received any committee or floor action, so weighing its real-world cost is moot.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was filed, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended in early January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Smith introduced the Community and Technical College Investment Act of 2022 in the House on September 29, 2022, with two Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, which was its last action.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote followed, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one lost anything the bill would have taken away, but the adults without credentials the bill was written for gained nothing. For-profit colleges and institutions that charge tuition were spared the competition from free public community college, and federal taxpayers were spared the open-ended cost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters gained nothing; the tuition status quo held

for.name: Rep. Adam Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 29, 2022 and it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the same day.

for.name: 2 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 29, 2022 and never took it up; no hearing, markup, or vote was held before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only a Democrat sponsoring the bill with two Democratic cosponsors and no votes or public opposition, so no partisan split can be measured — the bill simply never advanced far enough to draw one.

industries.note: The bill would make them tuition-free and fund them to expand capacity, hire counselors and navigators, and serve more low-income and adult students. As public institutions, their gain runs directly with students' gain.

A free public alternative for adults without credentials could pull enrollment and revenue away from colleges charging tuition. Their interest in the bill's fate runs against students' interest in lower costs.

industries.industry: Minority-serving, HBCU, Tribal, and rural-serving institutions
industries.note: The institutional capacity grant program directs subgrants toward historically Black, Hispanic-serving, Tribal, minority-serving, and rural-serving institutions and colleges in high-poverty areas, funding supports that help their students stay enrolled and finish credentials.
